nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.
nodes.title: Comparison bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and let $x \ne y$ be values. Then $y$ occurs in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ exactly as many times as it occurs in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap insertion leaves other multiplicities unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is one more than its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap insertion adds one copy of the inserted value

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ equals the result of sifting up position $i$ in the array obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry at position $i$ with $x$.
nodes.title: Array of a binary heap after decrease-key

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $a_i$ and adding one occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Multiset of a binary heap after decrease-key

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot position is at least the entry at its parent position.
nodes.title: Decrease-key yields a heap-ordered array

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ has the same length as $a$.
nodes.title: Decrease-key preserves the heap size

nodes.summary: Given a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, an index $i < |a|$ and a value $x \le a_i$, decrease-key returns the heap whose array is obtained from $a$ by replacing the entry at position $i$ with $x$ and then sifting position $i$ up, repeatedly swapping the entry with its parent while it is strictly smaller than the parent.
nodes.title: Decrease-key in a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$ added.
nodes.title: Elements after binary heap insertion

nodes.summary: The multiset of elements of a binary min-heap is the multiset of the entries of its level-order storage array, counted with multiplicity.
nodes.title: Elements of a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: The empty binary min-heap is the min-heap whose level-order storage array has no entries.
nodes.title: Empty binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, if sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ counts $c$ comparisons and $s$ swaps, then $c + s \le 2 \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Combined comparison and swap bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ equals the multiset of elements of $h'$ with one copy of $x$ added.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction splits off the minimum

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then every value $y \ne x$ occurs in the multiset of elements of $h'$ exactly as many times as in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction leaves other multiplicities unchanged

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of $h'$ is its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.
nodes.title: Binary heap extraction removes one copy of the minimum

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by erasing one occurrence of $x$.
nodes.title: Elements after binary heap extraction

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum of $h$ returns no result if and only if the level-order storage array of $h$ has size $0$.
nodes.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap fails exactly when it is empty

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x \le y$ for every value $y$ in the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is minimal

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type, and suppose extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$. Then every value $y \ne x$ is an element of $r$ if and only if it is an element of $h$.
nodes.title: Membership after extraction from a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is one of its elements

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then the level-order array of $r$ is heap ordered: every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry.
nodes.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap leaves a heap-ordered array

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extraction returns nothing when the level-order array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it returns the root entry (the first entry of the array) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root and restoring heap order.
nodes.title: Extracting the minimum of a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type whose level-order array is nonempty. If the array has exactly one entry, the result is the empty heap. Otherwise the last entry of the array replaces the root, the array shrinks by one, and the result is the heap obtained by sifting this entry down from the root.
nodes.title: Removing the root of a nonempty binary min-heap

nodes.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the left child of the node at index $i$ has index $2i + 1$.
nodes.title: Left child index in a level-order binary tree

nodes.summary: An array $a$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, is heap ordered when every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, where $|a|$ is the length of $a$, we have $a_{\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor} \le a_i$.
nodes.title: Heap order on a level-order array

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ of length $|a|$ and an index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ of $i$ is also less than $|a|$.
nodes.title: The parent of a valid nonroot index is valid

nodes.summary: In a binary tree stored in level order in an array indexed from $0$, the parent index of a natural number $i$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$, where $i - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so the root index $0$ is sent to $0$.
nodes.title: Parent index in a level-order binary tree

nodes.summary: In the level-order layout of a binary tree in an array indexed from $0$, the right child of the node at index $i$ is at index $2i + 2$.
nodes.title: Right child index in an array-backed binary tree

nodes.summary: For every natural number $i > 0$, the parent index $p = \lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ satisfies $\lfloor \log_2(p+1) \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$; that is, in the level-order binary tree the parent of a nonroot index lies one level above it.
nodes.title: The heap parent is one level up

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor = \lfloor \log_2 (i+1) \rfloor + 1$; that is, in the level-order binary tree stored in $a$, the node $c$ lies exactly one level below $i$.
nodes.title: The smaller child lies one level below its parent

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor \le \lfloor \log_2 |a| \rfloor$.
nodes.title: The smaller child's level is bounded by the array size

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns no value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has size $0$.
nodes.title: Binary heap minimum lookup fails exactly when empty

nodes.summary: A binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ is an array $a$ of elements of $\alpha$ (its level-order storage), of length $|a|$ and with entries $a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, that is heap ordered: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the entry $a_{\lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor}$ at the parent index of $i$ is at most $a_i$.
nodes.title: Binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns a value if and only if the storage array of $h$ has positive size.
nodes.title: Binary heap minimum lookup succeeds exactly when nonempty

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The binary heap minimum lookup is a lower bound

nodes.summary: Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.
nodes.title: The binary heap minimum lookup returns a stored element

nodes.summary: For a binary min-heap $h$, the minimum lookup returns the entry at index $0$ (the root) of the storage array of $h$ when that array is nonempty, and returns no value when it is empty.
nodes.title: Minimum lookup in a binary heap

nodes.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of entries of the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root equals the multiset of entries of $a$ with one occurrence of $a_0$ removed.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root removes the old root

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be a heap-ordered array over a linearly ordered type with at least two entries, and let $b$ be the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last entry to the root. Then $b$ is ready for sifting down at index $0$: index $0$ is valid in $b$, and for every index $j > 0$ of $b$ whose parent index $\lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ is not $0$, the entry of $b$ at the parent index is at most $b_j$.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root prepares a sift-down

nodes.summary: For a nonempty array $a$ of length $n$, this operation swaps the entries at indices $0$ and $n - 1$ and then deletes the final entry. The result has length $n - 1$; when $n \ge 2$ its entry at index $0$ is $a_{n-1}$ and its entry at each index $0 < i < n - 1$ is $a_i$.
nodes.title: Moving the last entry to the root

nodes.summary: For every binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the level-order array of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot index $i$ is at least the entry at its parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap preserves heap order

nodes.summary: If an array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered and $x$ is any value, then the array obtained by appending $x$ to $a$ satisfies the sift-up precondition at index $n$, the position of $x$: the only edge that may violate heap order is the one entering index $n$.
nodes.title: Appending to a heap-ordered array prepares it for sift-up

nodes.summary: To insert a value $x$ into a binary min-heap $h$, append $x$ at the end of the level-order array of $h$ and sift it up from its index (the old length of the array), repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it is smaller. The result is again a binary min-heap.
nodes.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array returned by timed sift-down from $i$, with its cost discarded, equals the array returned by sift-down from $i$.
nodes.title: Timed sift-down returns the sift-down result

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the array returned by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ equals the array returned by the plain sift-up of $a$ at $i$.
nodes.title: Counting does not change the result of sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the value returned by timed child selection at $i$, with its cost discarded, is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$ (an optional index, absent when $i$ has no valid child).
nodes.title: Timed child selection returns the smaller child

nodes.summary: If an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered, then $a_0 \le a_i$ for every valid index $i$ of $a$.
nodes.title: The root of a heap-ordered binary-heap array is minimal

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, timed sift-down returns an array together with a cost pair (value comparisons, array swaps), where costs add componentwise. If the left child index $2i+1$ is not a valid index of $a$, it returns $a$ at cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $c$ be the smaller child of $i$: the left child $2i+1$, unless the right child $2i+2$ is a valid index and…
nodes.title: Sift-down with comparison and swap counts

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $2 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Sift-down makes at most two comparisons per remaining level

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-down preserves the multiset of entries

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type that satisfies the sift-down precondition at a valid index $i$: the only edges that may violate heap order are those leaving $i$, and moving either child of $i$ up to position $i$ keeps the edge entering $i$ ordered. Then the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is heap-ordered.
nodes.title: Sift-down restores heap order

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-down permutes the array

nodes.summary: For an array $a$ over a type ordered by $\le$, write $p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/2 \rfloor$ for the parent of index $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-down at index $i$ when $i$ is a valid index of $a$; $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) \ne i$; and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with $p(j) = i$.
nodes.title: Sift-down precondition

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $\max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Sift-down performs at most one swap per remaining level

nodes.summary: Write $|a|$ for the size of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value comparisons plus the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $3 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.
nodes.title: Total sift-down cost is at most three per remaining level

nodes.summary: Sifting down an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type from index $i$ works as follows. If $i$ has a child in $a$, that is, if $2i+1$ is a valid index, let $c$ be the child of $i$ (among $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, if valid) holding the smaller value, preferring the left child $2i+1$ on ties. If $a_c < a_i$, swap the entries at $i$ and $c$ and continue sifting down from $c$; otherwise, or if $i$ has no child, return the…
nodes.title: Sift-down

nodes.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and an index $i$, this computes the sift-up of $a$ at $i$ together with a cost $(c, s) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $c$ counts value comparisons and $s$ counts swaps. If $i \ge |a|$ or $i = 0$, the result is $a$ with cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$. If $a_i < a_p$, the result is this sift-up…
nodes.title: Sift-up with comparison and swap counts

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.
nodes.title: Binary-heap sift-up preserves the multiset of entries

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let $i$ be an index such that $a$ is ready for sift-up at $i$. Then the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is heap ordered.
nodes.title: Sift-up restores heap order

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.
nodes.title: Sift-up permutes the array

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed from $0$, and for $j > 0$ let $p(j) = \lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-up at an index $i$ when $i < |a|$, when $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every $j \ne i$ with $0 < j < |a|$, and when, if $i > 0$, also $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) = i$.
nodes.title: Arrays ready for sift-up

nodes.summary: Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and an index $i$, the sift-up of $a$ from $i$ is defined by recursion on $i$. If $i = 0$ or $i \ge |a|$, the result is $a$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$; if $a_i < a_p$, the result is the sift-up from $p$ of the array obtained from $a$ by exchanging the entries at positions $i$ and $p$, and…
nodes.title: Sift-up

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $i < c$.
nodes.title: The smaller child has a larger index

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $c$ is less than the length $|a|$ of $a$.
nodes.title: The smaller child is a valid index

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$, and let $i$ be an index with children $\ell = 2i + 1$ and $r = 2i + 2$. If $\ell \ge |a|$, then $i$ has no smaller child. Otherwise the smaller child of $i$ is $r$ when $r < |a|$ and $a_r < a_\ell$, and $\ell$ in every other case, so ties go to the left child.
nodes.title: Smaller child

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$, the number of swaps counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.
nodes.title: Swap bound for sift-up

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be an index with $|a| \le 2i+1$, so that the left child of $i$ is not a valid index (this includes invalid indices $i$). Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from a leaf costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be a natural number with $|a| \le i$. Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from an invalid index costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then sift-down from $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$: it makes no value comparisons and no array swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-down from a node without children costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$ with $i \ge |a|$, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-up at an out-of-range index costs nothing

nodes.summary: For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type, sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $0$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.
nodes.title: Sift-up at the root costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no child, then the timed child selection at $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$.
nodes.title: Child selection at a node without children costs nothing

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, and count cost as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). The timed child selection at $i$ in $a$ has cost $(1, 0)$ if the right child index $2i + 2$ is less than the size of $a$, and cost $(0, 0)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Cost of child selection

nodes.summary: Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an index, with left child $2i + 1$ and right child $2i + 2$; cost is counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). If both children are valid indices of $a$, the selection costs $(1, 0)$ and returns the right child when its value is strictly less than the value at the left child, and the left child otherwise. If only the left child is a valid index,…

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
